chapters.title: Good Is the Enemy of Great
chapters.hook: A chipped mug beside a good dashboard can hide the first inch of drift.
chapters.counterintuition: Most leaders assume failure is the main danger because failure hurts and demands a response. The quieter danger is acceptable performance, because it gives everyone a reason to postpone the harder test of whether the system is truly building strength. The paradox is that the less dramatic move often protects the stronger result.

chapters.keyTakeaway: Good becomes dangerous when it lowers the pressure to test reality, compare against a harder standard, and build a pattern that lasts after the exciting moment fades.

A good organization can drift because each small compromise looks reasonable. One softened fact, one wrong seat, one attractive side path, one tool bought from fear, one reset made too soon. None of these choices announces itself as a collapse.

examples.title: Derek turns the chipped mug beside the yellow dashboard

planSpec.domain: a grocery district manager reading a good-enough dashboard before sunrise
planSpec.audience: a manager whose stores look stable while shoppers drift away
planSpec.stakes: whether acceptable numbers hide deeper loss
planSpec.requiredBeat: he sees every metric is fine and decides whether to cancel the hard customer visit

examples.scenario: At 6:18 a.m., Derek turns a chipped mug beside the dashboard in the Glen Park grocery office. Every tile is yellow, not red: sales flat, shrink flat, complaints low. Rain ticks against the back door. His cursor hovers over the calendar invite to cancel the rival-market visit. He has to decide whether fine is enough evidence to stay comfortable. A forklift beeps twice outside the door, and the sound makes the easy answer feel even easier because everyone wants the line moving again.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the store walk. Treat the yellow dashboard as a question, not a verdict, and compare the good-enough numbers with what customers are doing across the street.
examples.whyItMatters: Acceptable numbers can mute the pressure to learn. The visit tests whether the system is gaining strength or merely avoiding visible pain.

examples.title: Carmen asks what the blue binder is hiding

planSpec.domain: a school board retreat where acceptable scores are used to quiet concern
planSpec.audience: a board chair trying to raise the bar without insulting teachers
planSpec.stakes: whether decent scores hide family flight
planSpec.requiredBeat: she interrupts a self-congratulatory score review with a harder comparison question

examples.scenario: Tuesday, 10:07 a.m., Carmen stands beside a blue binder in the Pine Hollow library while the board president says, "We are above state average again." The projector hums. "Above which districts?" Carmen asks. "The ones our families choose when they leave?" Her thumb is on the next slide, a scatterplot of transfers. She must decide whether to soften the question. The page corner is damp from a coffee ring, and two people are already stacking chairs as if the decision has been made.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the harder comparison on the screen. Ask the board to define the rival standard before anyone celebrates the average that makes them feel safe.
examples.whyItMatters: Good feels different when compared with the right peer. A weak comparison flatters the room and lets the real loss keep moving quietly.

examples.title: Iris replays the gala total under the lilies

planSpec.domain: a nonprofit director after a record gala driven by one surprise check
planSpec.audience: a director who wants to know whether a big night changed the engine
planSpec.stakes: whether the team mistakes a spike for durable donor strength
planSpec.requiredBeat: she reconstructs the night and sees the single check that made the total misleading

examples.scenario: At 11:32 p.m., Iris sits alone in the hotel ballroom with lily petals stuck to the donation cards. The gala total on the screen is the largest in the shelter history. She sorts the pledge slips and finds the truth: one surprise check made the night look like a breakthrough. The monthly donor table is almost empty. She circles the repeat-gift count for tomorrow. The oven fan clicks off behind the prep table, leaving enough quiet for the missed step to feel much louder than the apology.
examples.whatToDo: Name the record total and then separate the spike from the engine. Ask what repeat behavior changed, not just what number looked exciting.
examples.whyItMatters: A one-night windfall can fund relief without proving momentum. Duration and repeated action show whether the system is stronger.

examples.title: Gwen stops relaunching the clinic brochure

planSpec.domain: a clinic administrator replacing monthly relaunches with one patient-flow measure
planSpec.audience: an administrator tired of fresh campaigns that do not improve wait times
planSpec.stakes: whether visible activity keeps resetting the same weak system
planSpec.requiredBeat: she contrasts loud relaunches with one repeated improvement measure

examples.scenario: Thursday, 4:46 p.m., Gwen peels last months clinic brochure from the corkboard, the tape tearing a strip of paint. Before, she announced a new access campaign every four weeks and the lobby still filled by 8:15. After the third reset, she kept one measure on the whiteboard: minutes from sign-in to first nurse contact. The posters looked dull, but the chairs stopped filling. A driver scrapes ice from the windshield outside, and the old route card curls at the edges under the fluorescent light.
examples.whatToDo: Fund the measure, not the slogan. Keep improving the same patient-flow step until the gain lasts long enough to show real strength.
examples.whyItMatters: Fresh stories can feel like progress while they reset attention. Repeated pressure on the same useful step lets momentum show up in the room.

examples.title: Luis tests the good launch with the refund bin

planSpec.domain: a software founder after a praised launch with hidden refund requests
planSpec.audience: a founder tempted to treat attention as proof
planSpec.stakes: whether launch heat hides a product that does not hold users
planSpec.requiredBeat: he predicts retention from applause and then opens the refund queue

examples.scenario: Friday, 2:05 p.m., Luis stands by the snack shelf while launch confetti clings to the carpet. The blog post went viral. Investors emailed. He predicts trial users will stick. Then support opens the refund bin on the monitor: forty-three requests, most from teams that praised the demo. His finger rests on the celebration email. He must decide what the launch proved. A cart wheel squeaks past the hand-sanitizer stand while the wrong forms sit in plain view between the two trays.
examples.whatToDo: Call the team around the churn list. Compare applause with held usage before naming the launch a win.
examples.whyItMatters: Attention is not the same as durable use. Refunds reveal whether the product changed behavior after the first bright moment passed.

examples.title: Mei watches the applause fade after demo day

planSpec.domain: a maker after a public demo that drew praise but no repeat orders
planSpec.audience: a solo founder trying to resist calling praise a breakthrough
planSpec.stakes: whether public applause hides a weak order pattern
planSpec.requiredBeat: she notices the applause and the empty reorder sheet in the same minute

examples.scenario: Saturday, 5:28 p.m., Mei folds the canvas banner at the craft fair while applause from her product demo fades into food-truck noise. Her phone is full of kind messages. The reorder sheet on the table has two names. She wants to post that the booth changed everything. Instead she studies the ink smudge where people handled the pen and walked away. The drain cover glints under the last lane rope, and the echo in the room makes a small delay feel like a secret.
examples.whatToDo: Write down the harder evidence before posting the victory. Track reorders, referrals, and repeat use, then let those numbers decide what the demo meant.
examples.whyItMatters: Praise can warm the ego while leaving the engine unchanged. Repeat behavior is the cleaner test of whether something is starting to build.

choices: Name the fact plainly and connect it to the next action
Hide the fact until morale improves
Replace the fact with a hopeful story
questions.explanation: Plain truth tied to action protects morale better than evasion. People can handle reality when it is usable.

choices: Practice the announcement

Collect more options without judging any
questions.explanation: The hour should make the decision cleaner. More options or a better announcement can wait until the standard is clear.

questions.prompt: Someone says the disciplined choice feels less impressive. Which answer is most accurate? The quieter choice will be harder to explain because it does not look like a launch, a rescue, or a bold public turn.
choices: Impressive is always the wrong goal
Less impressive choices are always safer
The right choice may look quieter because it protects compounding strength
questions.explanation: The point is not to avoid impressive moves. The point is to protect the pattern that can keep building.

questions.prompt: A team repeats the same mistake after praise or pressure changes the mood. Which intervention is best? The mistake happened after praise changed the mood, and the team is starting to treat the old habit as optional.
choices: Return to the habit or standard that produced the earlier strength
Add three new priorities to renew energy
Avoid talking about the mistake so people stay positive
questions.explanation: The strongest intervention reconnects the team to the source of strength before drift becomes normal.

questions.prompt: A leader is unsure whether a new tool, person, or project belongs. Which question should decide? The new option has a vendor demo, a confident owner, and a real price tag, but fit is still unclear.
choices: Will this be easy to defend politically?
Does this reinforce the system we are trying to build?
Can this make us look current by Friday?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement is the useful test. Politics and appearance may matter, but they cannot decide the fit.

questions.prompt: Which personal-life transfer is strongest? The same pattern has started showing up at home: too many options, not enough protection for the habit that was working.
choices: Change goals whenever motivation dips
Treat every opportunity as a yes
Name the core habit and remove one attractive distraction
questions.explanation: The same lesson transfers to personal work: protect the repeatable source of strength and cut what scatters it.

reviewCards.front: A choice looks attractive but may scatter effort. What do you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the governing standard first, then test the choice against it before pressure or excitement sets the answer.

reviewCards.front: A room wants a louder move. What should you teach back?
reviewCards.back: Loud moves only help when they reinforce the system. Quiet moves can be stronger when they keep force pointed in one direction.

reviewCards.front: A win or crisis is changing behavior. What is the hard retrieval question?
reviewCards.back: Ask which habit, fact, person, or focus created strength, then protect that source before adding anything new.

reviewCards.front: A pressured room wants the comfortable answer. Which move should come back first?
reviewCards.back: Bring the decision back to the visible standard and the next concrete action. Comfort can be considered only after the standard has been named.

reviewCards.front: A strong result is making the team relax. What should you retrieve before drift starts?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the source of the result: the person, fact, focus, habit, or repeated push that created strength. Protect that source before adding anything new.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is turning Good Is the Enemy of Great into a concrete test at the moment of choice. You name what must be protected, then choose the action that strengthens the system instead of the action that merely feels safe or dramatic.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work decision starts to sprawl, then write the governing standard in one sentence before voting or replying.
If a health plan gets crowded, then keep the repeatable habit and cut one add-on that only creates noise.
If a personal project gets praised or pressured, then protect the practice that produced the progress.
If a relationship improves after a hard talk, then repeat the small behavior that made truth safer instead of assuming the win will last.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, apply Good Is the Enemy of Great to one live choice. Write the tempting move, the governing standard, and the next action that protects the source of strength.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review three choices and mark each as reinforcing, resetting, or drifting. Keep one reinforcing action and cut one drifting action.

choices: Impressive is always the wrong goal
Less impressive choices are always safer
The right choice may look quieter because it protects compounding strength
questions.explanation: The point is not to avoid impressive moves. The point is to protect the pattern that can keep building.

questions.prompt: A team repeats the same mistake after praise or pressure changes the mood. Which intervention is best? The mistake happened after praise changed the mood, and the team is starting to treat the old habit as optional.
choices: Return to the habit or standard that produced the earlier strength
Add three new priorities to renew energy
Avoid talking about the mistake so people stay positive
questions.explanation: The strongest intervention reconnects the team to the source of strength before drift becomes normal.

questions.prompt: A leader is unsure whether a new tool, person, or project belongs. Which question should decide? The new option has a vendor demo, a confident owner, and a real price tag, but fit is still unclear.
choices: Will this be easy to defend politically?
Does this reinforce the system we are trying to build?
Can this make us look current by Friday?
questions.explanation: Reinforcement is the useful test. Politics and appearance may matter, but they cannot decide the fit.

questions.prompt: Which personal-life transfer is strongest? The same pattern has started showing up at home: too many options, not enough protection for the habit that was working.
choices: Change goals whenever motivation dips
Treat every opportunity as a yes
Name the core habit and remove one attractive distraction
questions.explanation: The same lesson transfers to personal work: protect the repeatable source of strength and cut what scatters it.

reviewCards.front: A choice looks attractive but may scatter effort. What do you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the governing standard first, then test the choice against it before pressure or excitement sets the answer.

reviewCards.front: A room wants a louder move. What should you teach back?
reviewCards.back: Loud moves only help when they reinforce the system. Quiet moves can be stronger when they keep force pointed in one direction.

reviewCards.front: A win or crisis is changing behavior. What is the hard retrieval question?
reviewCards.back: Ask which habit, fact, person, or focus created strength, then protect that source before adding anything new.

reviewCards.front: A pressured room wants the comfortable answer. Which move should come back first?
reviewCards.back: Bring the decision back to the visible standard and the next concrete action. Comfort can be considered only after the standard has been named.

reviewCards.front: A strong result is making the team relax. What should you retrieve before drift starts?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the source of the result: the person, fact, focus, habit, or repeated push that created strength. Protect that source before adding anything new.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is turning From Good to Great to Built to Last into a concrete test at the moment of choice. You name what must be protected, then choose the action that strengthens the system instead of the action that merely feels safe or dramatic.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work decision starts to sprawl, then write the governing standard in one sentence before voting or replying.
If a health plan gets crowded, then keep the repeatable habit and cut one add-on that only creates noise.
If a personal project gets praised or pressured, then protect the practice that produced the progress.
If a relationship improves after a hard talk, then repeat the small behavior that made truth safer instead of assuming the win will last.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, apply From Good to Great to Built to Last to one live choice. Write the tempting move, the governing standard, and the next action that protects the source of strength.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review three choices and mark each as reinforcing, resetting, or drifting. Keep one reinforcing action and cut one drifting action.

memorableLines.why: Opens the idea through a concrete, surprising image that reverses what success means.

memorableLines.text: A good organization can drift because each small compromise looks reasonable. One softened fact, one wrong seat, one attractive side path, one tool bought from fear, one reset made too soon. None of these choices announces itself as a collapse.
memorableLines.why: The specificity of the list makes drift tangible—each mistake is named, so none can hide as small.

memorableLines.text: The point is not to impress the room. The point is to leave the system stronger after the room empties.
memorableLines.why: It's the chapter's actual punchline—a decision rule that reverses the instinct to perform rather than protect.
